source.title: Deep Ignorance: Filtering Pretraining Data Builds Tamper-Resistant Safeguards into Open-Weight LLMs
source.authors: Kyle O'Brien; Stephen Casper; Quentin Anthony; Tomasz Korbak; Robert Kirk; Xander Davies; Ishan Mishra; Geoffrey Irving; Yarin Gal; Stella Biderman

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether harmful fine-tuning and prompt-based attacks elicit harmful compliance, using different models and attack/evaluation setups from the original sources. It does not test first-token KL concentration or safety localization.
record.gate_note: The main experiments measure biothreat proxy knowledge, not chat refusal or harmful-request compliance, so those results are not rows for these claim versions. Section G reports jailbreak-robustness results for instruction-fine-tuned models from Maini et al. (2025). Numeric values in Figure 10 are flattened and cannot be assigned confidently to attack metrics; rows use only the paper’s explicit textual summaries.
record.test_reason: The main experiments measure biothreat proxy knowledge in non-chat base models, which no version covers. Section G is different: it runs harmful fine-tuning (full and LoRA) and GCG-U attacks on Maini et al.'s 1.7B instruction-tuned models, with and without pretraining filtering. It scores compliance with harmful requests using a StrongReject-style GPT-4o grader. That bears on V1 and, for GCG-U, on V4, in a new setting of data-filtered small models.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that pretraining data filtering durably suppresses precise biothreat knowledge under up to 10k steps of fine-tuning, but cannot block in-context retrieval. On Maini et al.'s models, filtering gives little protection against harmful fine-tuning and increases few-shot vulnerability. They hypothesize that filtering cannot durably suppress propensities such as compliance with harmful requests. They also report that CB and CB+LAT were effective against few-shot attacks in those models, while synthetic document training was not.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than measuring small-data fine-tuning of safety-trained chat models as in the cited work, the study evaluates attacks on Maini et al.’s 1.7B instruction-fine-tuned models, including full/LoRA fine-tuning on 3,900 harmful examples, prompting, and other attacks.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack type changes the reported result: filtered models are more vulnerable to few-shot prompting, while the models are described as fairly resistant to GCG-U and latent-space attacks.

fits_no_version.finding: A few-shot in-context jailbreak with harmful demonstrations raises compliance strongly. The original filtered model goes from 0.00 to 0.85 and the baseline from 0.16 to 0.67. The filtered variants are more vulnerable on average.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In-context harmful demonstrations (few- or many-shot) bypass refusal in safety-tuned models, and more so after pretraining filtering of harmful data.

fits_no_version.finding: Universal latent-space activation attacks barely raise compliance: about 0.00–0.08 on the original models.

record.code_released: The paper states that code and models are released; the URL is not stated in the provided text.
record.problems: Section G uses relatively small 1.7B models and reports the attack outcomes mainly in Figure 10; the flattened figure does not permit confident assignment of individual numbers to attack metrics. Fine-tuning attacks use 3,900 examples, outside the claim’s few-to-hundreds range. The authors caution that findings may not extend to larger state-of-the-art models.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for the main data-filtering and biothreat-knowledge evaluations: they measure knowledge rather than harmful-request refusal/compliance. No rows for benign WikiText fine-tuning, which measures proxy-knowledge retention rather than safety behavior. Figure 10 values were not extracted individually because the flattened layout does not support confident assignment.

untested.parts: Small-data regime (a few to a few hundred examples): only 3,900 examples over 1,218 steps were used. Large chat models were not tested.
Not tested for harmful compliance. Benign WikiText fine-tuning is evaluated only for biothreat knowledge in base models.
No prefilling of a compliant opening and no decoding-parameter attacks. Only universal GCG with 5 iterations was used.
Not tested. Section 6.2 speculates that propensities need no precise knowledge, which concerns filtering, not token-depth.
No token-depth safety training. Circuit Breaking and CB+LAT are tested but are not deep-alignment training.

missing.what: Per-defense fine-tuning results bearing on V1. CB goes from 0.00 to 0.51/0.56 (baseline) and 0.38/0.41 (filtered). CB+LAT goes from 0.00 to 0.57/0.55 (baseline) and 0.48/0.50 (filtered). SDT goes from 0.24–0.27 to 0.55–0.60. Defended models are still compromised by harmful fine-tuning.
Separate no-attack and attacked compliance values for baseline versus filtered models under each attack. The rows give only qualitative text.

record.verdict_notes: Figure 10 is flattened. I assigned the first line of each defense pair to the filtered models and the second to the baseline models. This matches the caption: few-shot averages 0.66 versus 0.35, and fine-tune averages about 0.51 versus 0.55. Columns read as General, No Attack, Fewshot, GCG-U, Latent, Full FT, LoRA FT. Numeric verdicts depend on this inference. Neither original source is this study. The tranche was changed from T2 to T3 because the result comes from a new setting (pretraining-filtered small models).

versions.untested_parts: The study uses 3,900 harmful examples and 1,218 fine-tuning steps, not a few to a few hundred examples; it does not establish near-total removal of refusal.
Benign WikiText fine-tuning is evaluated for retained biothreat proxy knowledge in the paper’s non-chat models, not harmful-request compliance or refusal.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL analysis across response positions.
No compliant-opening prefill or decoding-change experiment. The study tests few-shot, GCG-U, and latent-space jailbreak attacks; GCG-U uses a universal adversarial prompt, not a compliant opening.
No experiment localizes safety to a small set of weights or ranks.

The study discusses differences between suppressing precise knowledge and suppressing harmful propensities, but does not test why safety alignment is shallow or why safety changes occur at particular response positions.
No experiment trains safety to extend beyond initial response tokens.

rows.subject: Maini et al. (2025) baseline and filtered 1.7B models (aggregate comparison)
rows.operation_detail: Full and LoRA fine-tuning attacks using harmful prompt/completion pairs; five epochs on 3,900 examples, totaling 1,218 steps.

conditions.value: held-out 250 examples; GPT-4o and modified StrongReject autograder

rows.measure: Successful compliance with harmful requests / jailbreak robustness
rows.value: Filtered model was only slightly more resistant to fine-tuning attacks on average.
rows.note: The paper reports a qualitative aggregate comparison; flattened Figure 10 values are not assigned to full- versus LoRA-fine-tuning metrics. The tested attack uses more examples and steps than the claim’s few-to-hundreds range.
rows.check: The row measures the wrong contrast. It compares filtered against baseline robustness, but V1 asks whether harmful fine-tuning raises compliance over the no-attack level. Reading Figure 10 (assignment inferred, see notes): the original baseline model goes from 0.16 with no attack to 0.55 (full) and 0.54 (LoRA). The original filtered model goes from 0.00 to 0.56 and 0.57. Baseline should be 'no attack', not 'Maini baseline model'.

rows.subject: Maini et al. (2025) baseline and filtered 1.7B models (aggregate comparison)
rows.operation_detail: Few-shot jailbreak prompting using examples from the LAT Harmful Dataset.

conditions.value: held-out harmful requests; GPT-4o and modified StrongReject autograder

rows.measure: Successful compliance with harmful requests / jailbreak robustness
rows.value: Filtered model variants were substantially more vulnerable to few-shot prompting attacks on average.
rows.note: Qualitative comparison across model variants; no reliably assignable numeric rate is given in the text.
rows.check: This is a few-shot in-context jailbreak with harmful demonstrations. It is not a compliant-opening prefill, a suffix or a decoding change, so it does not measure V4. The row also records a filtered-versus-baseline comparison rather than a rate of the behaviour. Moved to fits_no_version.
